526.title: The moonlit ride
526.hook: King Ajatasattu, who killed his father, rides out on a full-moon night to ask what practice is good for
526.howItsDone: Uposatha, the observance day at the new and full moons (and in some traditions the quarter moons), is still kept in Theravada communities, when lay people often visit monasteries, take precepts and listen to teachings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the net of views, cast like a fisherman's, and your line, all views, in the net. Today, the second long discourse, and a night ride.

It's the full moon of the autumn month, an observance night. King Ajatasattu of Magadha sits on the upper terrace of his palace at Rajagaha, among his ministers, and says something almost tender: how lovely this moonlit night is. Which teacher could we visit tonight who might bring peace to my heart? Later in this discourse, the king will confess what he's carrying. Tradition says he seized the throne and had his own father, King Bimbisara, put to death. That's the man looking at the moon.
screen: `A FULL-MOON NIGHT IN RAJAGAHA.` → `PEACE TO MY HEART?` → `A KING WHO KILLED HIS FATHER.`

segments.voice: One by one, his ministers suggest famous teachers. Six of them. The king says nothing. One man on the terrace is silent too: Jivaka, the royal physician. Why so quiet, Jivaka? The Blessed One is staying in my mango grove, Jivaka says, with twelve hundred and fifty monks. Go and see him. So the king rides out: five hundred women on she-elephants, torches burning, the king on the royal elephant. Near the grove, he's suddenly afraid; his hair stands on end. Jivaka, are you handing me to my enemies? How can there be twelve hundred and fifty monks here, and not one sneeze, not one cough? Don't be afraid, great king, says Jivaka. Look, there are lamps burning in the pavilion. The king walks in and sees the whole community sitting utterly still, like a clear lake. I wish my son, Prince Udayibhadda, could have a calm like this, he says. Then he bows and asks his question. People in every trade get a visible fruit from their work: elephant riders, archers, cooks, barbers, bath attendants. They support their families with it. Can you show me a fruit of the contemplative life, visible here and now? That's the question the whole discourse answers. The Pali for the night he rode out is uposatha: the observance day, at the moon's turning. A troubled king, on a holy night, asking what practice is actually good for.
screen: `SIX TEACHERS SUGGESTED, KING SILENT` · `JIVAKA: GO TO MY MANGO GROVE` · `NOT ONE SNEEZE, NOT ONE COUGH` · `WHAT FRUIT, HERE AND NOW?` · then, large: `THE MOONLIT RIDE.`

segments.voice: Ask the king's question for yourself, honestly: is there a fruit of your practice you can see here and now, a little more patience, a quicker return from anger, a quieter night? Maybe nothing obvious yet, and either answer is fine; let the question sit, like a lamp in a dark grove.
Uposatha. The observance day, at the moon's turning: the night a troubled king rode out to ask what the contemplative life is good for.
Your line: like a clear lake. Twelve hundred and fifty monks, and not one cough. That's day five hundred twenty-six.

527.title: Six answers that dodge
527.hook: the king recounts six famous teachers; none answered his question
527.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use this passage to illustrate how the Buddha's contemporaries were remembered in Buddhist sources; Jain tradition preserves its own scriptures and account of Mahavira's teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday: uposatha, a silent grove, and your line, like a clear lake. Today the king explains why he's still asking.

You ask a simple question at the help desk: will my package arrive by Friday? And you get a long, confident answer about the history of shipping. Polite, maybe even brilliant. But it isn't an answer. King Ajatasattu has had that experience six times. When he asks the Buddha what the contemplative life is good for, the Buddha asks him back: have you asked anyone else? Yes, says the king. Six famous teachers. And he tells what each one said.
screen: `A SIMPLE QUESTION AT THE HELP DESK.` → `A BRILLIANT NON-ANSWER.` → `SIX TEACHERS, SIX TIMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the king's account. Purana Kassapa told him deeds bring no merit and no evil, whatever one does. Makkhali Gosala told him beings are purified only by wandering through countless lives, as fixed as a ball of string that unrolls to its end. Ajita of the hair blanket said nothing survives the body, which breaks into earth, water, fire and air. Pakudha Kaccayana said there are seven unchanging substances, so even a sword through a head only passes between them. Nigantha Nataputta told him about a fourfold restraint. And Sanjaya Belatthiputta wouldn't commit to anything: I don't say it's so, I don't say it's not so, I don't say it's neither. The texts call that eel-wriggling. Two things matter here. First, this is the king's summary, inside a Buddhist text. These teachers had their own followers, who would describe them in their own terms. Nigantha Nataputta is traditionally identified with Mahavira, whom Jains revere, and Jains have their own scriptures and understanding of his teaching. The discourse isn't a fair hearing of six philosophies, and doesn't claim to be. Second, the king's point: whatever their merits, none of them answered his question. He asked about a fruit visible here and now. It was like asking about a mango and being told about a breadfruit. And he didn't scold any of them; a king, he thought, shouldn't insult a renunciant in his own realm. He just got up and left, still carrying his question.

Your line: they didn't answer. He asked about a mango and was told about a breadfruit. Go gently.

528.title: The slave who went forth
528.hook: the first fruit: a slave who ordains is greeted with honor by the king himself
528.howItsDone: In Buddhist monastic communities, seniority is counted from the day of ordination rather than from birth or former status, and lay people of every rank bow to monastics, including kings in some Theravada countries.

segments.voice: Yesterday: eel-wriggling, six answers that dodge, and your line, they didn't answer. Today, at last, the king gets an answer.

The king has asked his question: what fruit does the contemplative life bring, visible here and now? The Buddha could answer with a lecture on meditation, or freedom, or the end of suffering. He doesn't. He answers with a question about the people in the king's own household. Great king, suppose there were a man in your service. Not a minister, not a guard. A slave.
screen: `WHAT FRUIT, HERE AND NOW?` → `NO LECTURE.` → `A QUESTION ABOUT THE KING'S HOUSEHOLD.`

segments.voice: He gets up before you and goes to bed after you. He does whatever you want, speaks to please you, and watches your face for your mood. And one day he thinks: this is strange. King Ajatasattu is a human being, and so am I. He lives like a god, and I live like this. Let me do something good with my life. Let me shave my head, put on the ochre robe, and go forth. And he does. He lives restrained in body, speech and mind, content with simple food and shelter, glad to be alone. Now suppose your people told you about him. Would you say: bring him back, make him my slave again? And the king answers, honestly: no, lord. We would bow to him, stand up when he came, offer him a seat, robes, food, a place to live and medicine, and see that he was protected. Then, the Buddha says, isn't that a fruit of the contemplative life, visible here and now? Yes, says the king. It is. That's the first fruit: samaññaphala. The Buddha goes on to a free farmer who pays his taxes, with the same result. Notice what the answer does. The king's own society, built on rank, already admits that this life changes how a person is seen. The man who watched the king's face now has the king rising for him. It doesn't erase the cruelty of that world. But inside it, a door opens, and the king himself can see it.

529.title: Wings are enough
529.hook: the renunciant is content like a bird that takes only its wings
529.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics traditionally keep only a few requisites (robes, bowl, and a small set of necessities), and contentment is taught to lay people too as a quality to cultivate alongside generosity.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samannaphala, the first fruit, and your line, honored. Today, the king hears what that new life is actually like.

Moving day. Boxes everywhere. Things forgotten under the bed, in the back of a closet, each one asking: keep me? And each one, kept, gets carried to the next place. Outside the window, a small bird sits on a branch. It takes off, carrying nothing but the wings it flies with. In the second long discourse, after the first fruits, the Buddha describes the monk's daily life, and lands on that bird.
screen: `MOVING DAY: BOXES EVERYWHERE.` → `A BIRD TAKES OFF.` → `NOTHING BUT ITS WINGS.`

segments.voice: He walks the king through the training step by step. First, the moral conduct, all those small things. Then guarding the senses: seeing a form, not grabbing at its features. Then mindfulness and clear knowing in everything: walking forward and back, looking ahead and to the side, bending and stretching, eating and drinking, even in the toilet, falling asleep and waking. And then this. How, great king, is a monk content? He's content with a robe to protect his body and almsfood to keep his stomach going, and wherever he goes, he takes only these. Just as a bird, wherever it flies, flies with its wings as its only burden. The Pali word is santutthi: contentment, being satisfied with what's enough. It's not total poverty. He has a robe and a bowl; the bird has wings. It isn't a contest to own nothing. It's carrying only what the flight needs. Then someone with this virtue, restraint, mindfulness and contentment goes to a quiet place, a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain cave, sits cross-legged, and sets mindfulness in front. That's where the next fruits begin. The order matters. Contentment comes before the deep meditation, not after. A mind still packing and unpacking boxes can't sit still under a tree. And the Buddha offers this lightness to a king who owns elephants, palaces and an army, as a fruit visible here and now.

segments.voice: Notice what you're carrying right now, tension in the shoulders, a plan for later, a worry from this morning, and name each one gently. Ask whether this flight needs it, and if not, set it down for the length of the sit: a body, a breath, wings.
Santutthi. Contentment, being satisfied with what's enough, like a bird with its wings as its only burden.
Your line: only what the flight needs. A robe, a bowl, a pair of wings. See you tomorrow.

530.title: The clear gem
530.hook: the jhana similes, and a clear gem with a thread seen through it
530.howItsDone: Meditation teachers in several Buddhist traditions use the four jhana similes from this discourse to describe deepening concentration, and then guide practitioners to turn the settled mind toward seeing body and mind clearly.

segments.voice: Yesterday: santutthi, a bird with only its wings, and your line, only what the flight needs. Today the monk sits down under the tree.

Hold a clear marble or a glass bead up to the light, and you can see right through it. If a thread runs through the middle, you see the thread too, its color, how it bends. Nothing is hidden. The second long discourse ends its account of meditation with an object like that: a gem, cut and polished, so clear that the thread strung through it is plain to see. But first, four pictures of a mind settling.
screen: `A GLASS BEAD HELD TO THE LIGHT.` → `THE THREAD INSIDE, PLAIN TO SEE.` → `FIRST, FOUR PICTURES.`

segments.voice: The monk has set down the five hindrances, and joy arises. Then come the four absorptions, the jhanas, each with a picture. In the first, joy and ease soak through the whole body, like a bath attendant kneading soap powder with water until the ball of powder is moist all through, and nothing drips. In the second, like a deep lake fed by a spring from underneath, no stream flowing in, no rain: cool water wells up from within and fills it. In the third, like lotuses growing underwater, never breaking the surface, soaked from root to tip. In the fourth, like someone sitting wrapped head to foot in a clean white cloth, no part of the body uncovered. Then the mind is concentrated, purified, bright, workable, steady, and the monk turns it toward knowing. This body is made of the four elements, born of mother and father, kept going by rice and porridge, bound to wear away and break apart. And this consciousness of mine rests on it and is tied to it. Here's the gem. A beautiful veluriya, a beryl, eight-faceted, well cut, clear and flawless, and through it runs a thread: blue, yellow, red, white or brown. Someone with good eyes takes it in hand and sees: this is the gem, and this is the thread running through it. That's the image of insight here. Not a vision of something far away. Just seeing, clearly, what's already in your hand: a body, and the awareness strung through it.
screen: `SOAP POWDER, SOAKED THROUGH` · `A LAKE FED FROM BELOW` · `LOTUSES UNDER WATER, A WHITE CLOTH` · `THE GEM, AND THE THREAD THROUGH IT` · then, large: `THE GEM AND THE THREAD.`

segments.voice: Feel the body as one whole shape, sitting here, weight, warmth, breath: that's the gem. Now notice the knowing of it, the thread, without trying to separate the two; when you drift, come back to the shape, and the knowing.
Veluriya. A beryl, flawless and clear: a settled mind sees the body and the consciousness running through it, as plainly as a thread through this gem.
Your line: the gem and the thread. Nothing hidden, nothing far away. Day five hundred thirty.

531.title: The king's regret
531.hook: Ajatasattu confesses; the Buddha says had he not killed his father he would have seen the truth that night
531.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics confess offenses to one another in regular ceremonies, and lay Buddhists in some traditions acknowledge wrongdoing and renew their precepts, following the pattern in DN 2: seeing a wrong as wrong, making amends, and resolving restraint.

segments.voice: Yesterday: veluriya, and your line, the gem and the thread. Today the long night in the mango grove ends.

The teaching is over. The Buddha has walked the king all the way from the honored slave to the end of the taints. The lamps are still burning in the pavilion. And King Ajatasattu, who rode out because he wanted peace in his heart, does two things. First he says the familiar words that close these discourses: excellent, as if something overturned had been set upright. He goes for refuge. And then he says what he came carrying.
screen: `THE LAMPS STILL BURNING.` → `EXCELLENT, LIKE SOMETHING SET UPRIGHT.` → `THEN, WHAT HE CAME CARRYING.`

segments.voice: Lord, he says, a transgression overcame me. Foolish, confused and unskillful as I was, for the sake of the throne, I took the life of my father, a good man, a righteous king. May the Blessed One accept my confession, so that I may restrain myself in the future. The Pali word is accaya: a transgression, a going beyond the line. The Buddha's answer is direct. Yes, great king, a transgression overcame you. He doesn't soften the deed. But since you see it as a transgression, and make amends in line with the dhamma, we accept it. For this is growth in the noble discipline: to see a wrong as wrong, make amends, and restrain yourself in the future. The king rises, bows, and leaves. And then the Buddha says something to the monks that is hard to hear. This king is wounded, damaged. If he had not taken his father's life, the clear eye of the dhamma would have opened in him tonight, on that very seat. The discourse holds two things at once. Confession is real, and welcomed; it's called growth, not humiliation. And the deed is real too; it has left a mark that one honest night can't remove. The king came for peace of heart and received something more sober: the path is still open to him, but he will walk it carrying what he did. Later tradition remembers Ajatasattu as a supporter of the community. The canon doesn't pretend the night erased the past. It just doesn't close the door.
screen: `I TOOK MY FATHER'S LIFE` · `SEEN AS WRONG, WE ACCEPT IT` · `THIS IS GROWTH IN THE DISCIPLINE` · `HE WOULD HAVE SEEN, BUT FOR THAT` · then, large: `REGRET, CONFESSED.`

segments.voice: Choose a small regret, something you can hold without being flooded, and name it plainly to yourself, with no excuses and no punishment: I did this. Then rest with the three steps from the text, seeing it as a mistake, making amends if there's a way, intending to do differently, and let it simply be seen while you breathe.
Accaya. A transgression, a going beyond the line: the king's wrong, seen as wrong, confessed and accepted as growth, while the deed still leaves its mark.
Your line: regret, confessed. Seeing a wrong as wrong is where growth begins. Rest well.

532.title: Pride of birth
532.hook: a proud young brahmin insults the Sakyans, and his own ancestry comes out
532.carry: no talk of birth at the summit
532.howItsDone: In Buddhist monastic communities, people from every background ordain together, and order is counted from ordination, not birth; the teaching that conduct, not lineage, makes a person noble is repeated across the discourses.

segments.voice: Yesterday: accaya, a wrong seen as wrong, and your line, regret, confessed. Today ends a week, with a young man very proud of his family.

A famous brahmin teacher named Pokkharasati wants to know if the Buddha is really who people say. So he sends his student, Ambattha, a young man who has mastered the Vedas. Ambattha arrives and doesn't sit down. He walks around while the Buddha sits, talking at him. And when the Buddha asks if that's how he speaks to elders, Ambattha starts on the Sakyans, the Buddha's own clan. Once, he says, I went to their assembly hall in Kapilavatthu, and they laughed, and nobody offered me a seat. They're menials.
screen: `POKKHARASATI SENDS HIS STUDENT.` → `AMBATTHA WON'T SIT DOWN.` → `THE SAKYANS LAUGHED AT ME.`

segments.voice: The Buddha's first reply is gentle. Even a little quail can chirp as it likes in its own nest; Kapilavatthu is the Sakyans' home. But Ambattha insults them again, and again. So the Buddha asks a simple question: what's your clan? Kanhayana, says Ambattha. And the Buddha tells the old story. The Sakyans trace their line to an ancient king, Okkaka. That king had a slave woman, and she had a son named Kanha. Ambattha's clan descends from him. By the standards Ambattha himself has been using, his own ancestor was the son of a slave in the Sakyans' royal house. Ambattha won't answer at first. The text says a spirit holding a thunderbolt appeared above him, and he finally admits: yes, that's what my teachers say. His fellow students start jeering. And here's the turn. The Buddha stops them. Don't look down on Ambattha, he says. That Kanha became a great sage, and a king gave him his own daughter in marriage. So the story doesn't end as a humiliation. Read this way, it shows that pride of birth falls apart when you look closely. The Pali word is jati: birth. Then the teaching. In the highest knowledge and conduct, there's no talk of birth, no talk of clan, no talk of who is worthy of whom. That talk belongs to marriages and family arrangements. Look back at the week: the moonlit ride, the dodging answers, honored, wings, the gem and thread, regret confessed. And now a family tree, shaken.
screen: `A QUAIL CHIRPS IN ITS OWN NEST` · `WHAT'S YOUR CLAN?` · `DON'T LOOK DOWN ON HIM` · `NO TALK OF BIRTH AT THE SUMMIT` · then, large: `PRIDE OF BIRTH.`

segments.voice: If a pride of family comes to mind, our people, our name, our side of town, our school, hold it gently and notice any small lift it gives. Then picture the family tree going back past anyone you know, to people of every kind, and let the lift soften; you can keep loving your family and just set down the ranking.
Jati. Birth, also the group one is born into: it matters to marriages and family trees, and not at all to knowledge and good conduct.
Your line: no talk of birth at the summit. What counts there is knowledge and conduct. Day five hundred thirty-two, done.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit jati: birth, also the group one is born into. the ground of Ambattha's pride.

chat.meaning: Ambattha's pride falls apart when the old story is told. In the highest knowledge and conduct, the Buddha says, there's no talk of birth or clan.
